title: SSi dialogue codex: the 12 sentence-grain conversational frames (D1-D12)
purpose: The definitions a model (Haiku family) uses to say which conversational frames a pod TURN instantiates. Tom 2026-10-07 (r-2026-10-07-never-use-regex-to-classify-language): classified by a model reading these definitions, never by regex. The D-ids are stable and pinned to tools/frame-layer/dialogue-patterns.cjs, which keeps each frame's fixed_material, position and shape_nodes as data.
task: You tag turns from a spoken-dialogue corpus (a language course's conversation pods, and clinical health-sector conversations) with conversational frames
request: For EACH numbered turn, give the D-frame ids it instantiates, per the codex. Never output O: this codex has no openers.
general_rules: A frame is a CONVERSATIONAL MOVE: what the speaker is DOING with these words in the conversation (greeting, thanking, apologising, handing something over). Judge the move, never the presence of a word. 'Thank you very much. Goodbye.' fires D3 and D1; 'thanks to the rain we stayed in' fires nothing.

A turn is often several sentences. Check EVERY sentence of the turn against EVERY frame and fire each frame that any sentence instantiates. 'Hello! I'm sorry but I can't talk at the moment.' fires D1 and D4.

Only the speaker's OWN move counts. A greeting, thanks or apology that is reported, quoted, described or talked about does not fire: 'I said hello to her', 'my mother always said thank you', 'say sorry to your brother'.
Multi-label: fire every frame the turn genuinely instantiates; many turns fire none ('I'm from Manchester.', 'It's not very far.').

The text may also be a phrase from a language course rather than a pod turn, and its language may not be English (a course's known side). Apply the same moves: Welsh 'diolch' is thanks (D3), Spanish 'perdone' is an attention-getter (D4).
Placeholders like [target language] or stage directions in brackets are part of the text; ignore them for tagging.
When unsure whether a borderline case fires, follow the frame's boundary rules; if they do not settle it, do not fire.
output: One line per turn: '<number>: <tokens>' where tokens are D-frame ids, or '-' when there is nothing. Example: '12: D3 D1'.

frames.name: ritual open/close
frames.definition: The speaker ritually OPENS or CLOSES an encounter: a greeting (hello, hi, good morning/afternoon/evening, welcome, pleased/nice/lovely to meet you) or a farewell (goodbye, bye, good night, see you later/tomorrow/then, take care as a parting).
positives: Good morning, Sarah!
Thank you very much. Goodbye.
Yes, very. I'm very tired now. Good night. See you tomorrow.
Hello, my name's Siân, I'm one of the nurses looking after you today.
How interesting. Well, lovely to meet you.

near_misses.text: Did you have a good morning?
near_misses.why: asks about the morning; not a greeting

near_misses.text: I said hello to her at the station.
I'll see you at the station at six.
near_misses.why: arranges a meeting; not a parting formula

near_misses.text: Welcome back is what the sign says.
Good, now breathe in for me.

boundary: 'See you then/later/tomorrow' closing a turn is a farewell and fires.
'Pleased to meet you (too)' and 'lovely to meet you' are ritual and fire.
'Good night' fires; 'a good night's sleep' does not.

frames.name: polar response + elaboration
frames.definition: A sentence of the turn OPENS with a polar answer particle that answers or responds to the other speaker: yes, no, yeah, yep, nope, of course, certainly, absolutely, definitely, I'm afraid not, afraid so, sure (as a yes). Usually followed by an elaboration, but a bare particle counts.
positives: Yes, I've got a busy day today.
No, it's free. Please, go ahead.
Yes, please.
Of course. There's the machine.
No, I'm sorry, I'm busy tomorrow.

near_misses.text: No one came to the party.
near_misses.why: 'no one' is a pronoun, not an answer particle

near_misses.text: With milk but with no sugar.

near_misses.why: a reassurance / downgrade (D11, D7), not a polar answer

near_misses.text: I said yes to the job.

near_misses.why: the particles are talked about, not used to answer

boundary: The particle must open a sentence of the turn and work as an answer or response.
'Of course' fires D2 when it grants or agrees ('Of course. Would you like...'); it may also fire D7 when it is uptake of what was said.
'No problem' / 'no worries' are NOT D2.

frames.name: thanks / gratitude
frames.definition: The speaker THANKS the other or expresses gratitude: thank you, thanks, cheers (as thanks), much obliged, I appreciate it, that's very kind of you, thank goodness (relief-gratitude).
positives: Thank you very much. Goodbye.
I'm very well, thank you.
Righto. Thank you, love.
Thanks, that's really helpful.
That's very kind of you.

near_misses.text: Thanks to the rain, we stayed in.
Say thank you to your grandmother.
near_misses.why: an instruction to thank someone else
describes a third person; no gratitude

near_misses.text: The thank-you cards are on the table.

boundary: 'No, thank you' (a polite refusal) fires D3 (and D2).
Relief formulas 'thank goodness/God' fire.
'That's very kind of you' fires only when said to the interlocutor as thanks.

frames.name: apology / attention-getter
frames.definition: The speaker APOLOGISES or GETS ATTENTION with a formula at the start of a sentence: excuse me, sorry, I'm sorry, pardon (me), forgive me. Includes 'Sorry?' / 'Pardon?' as a request to repeat.
positives: Excuse me, is this seat taken?
Hello! I'm sorry but I can't talk at the moment.
I'm sorry, I didn't understand you.
Sorry, could you say that again?
Excuse me. Hello. What's your name?

near_misses.text: I'm sorry to hear about your mother.

boundary: Must be the speaker's own apology or attention-getter, normally opening a sentence.
Sympathy ('sorry to hear that', 'sorry for your loss') does NOT fire.

frames.name: deictic handover
frames.shape: here's [NP] | here you are | here it is | there's [NP]
frames.definition: The speaker HANDS OVER or PRESENTS a physical thing in the situation, pointing at it: here you are, here it is, here's your coffee, here are the keys, there's the machine, there's your table.
positives: Here's your coffee.
Here you are.
Of course. There's the machine.
Here's your medication and your discharge sheet.
Here are the tickets, two singles.

near_misses.why: presents an idea, not a thing

near_misses.text: There's a problem with my room.
Here we are, the station at last.
near_misses.why: announces arrival; nothing presented to the other

boundary: Fires only for an object physically given or pointed out to the other in the situation.
Existential 'there is/are' does not fire.

frames.name: reciprocal return
frames.definition: The speaker RETURNS the same question to the other, normally after answering it: and you?, and yourself?, what about you?, how about you?, and what do you do? (when it returns the question just asked).
positives: My name is Anna. And you?
I'm from Manchester, but I live in London now. And you?
Yes, of course. I'm a nurse. It's near here. And what do you do?
Not bad, thanks. What about you?
I'm fine. And yourself?

near_misses.text: I'm here with my wife and children.
How about we go on Saturday?
You and your brother should come.
And you can sit by the window.

near_misses.why: raises a new topic, not a return

boundary: The question must be addressed back to the other and be the same question (or the same topic) they asked or would be asked.

frames.name: uptake assessment
frames.definition: A sentence OPENS with a short evaluative uptake of what the other just said or did: excellent, lovely, perfect, great, wonderful, brilliant, marvellous, no problem, that's fine, good idea, exactly, how interesting, well done.
positives: How interesting. Well, lovely to meet you.
Perfect, I'll take it.
Excellent choice.
Of course, no problem at all.
Lovely. Now hold still for me.

near_misses.why: assesses the world, not the other's turn, and does not open the sentence
assessment inside a report, not uptake

boundary: The assessment opens a sentence and reacts to the previous turn or the situation just created.
'Well done' as praise of the other also fires D7 (and may fire D11 if it reassures).

frames.name: ellipted order
frames.definition: An ORDER or REQUEST made with a noun phrase and 'please' but NO verb: the ellipsis is the frame. 'Two Americanos and a cup of tea, please.' 'A table for two, please.' 'Large, please.'
positives: Good morning. Two Americanos and a cup of tea, please.
Four single tickets to town, please.
A table for two, please.
Just the bill, please.
Large, please.

near_misses.why: a bare acceptance, no ordered item

near_misses.text: Can I have a glass of water, please?
Tea, coffee and sandwiches are served at four.

boundary: No finite or imperative verb in the ordering sentence.
The ordered item must be named.

frames.name: reckoning
frames.definition: The speaker STATES THE AMOUNT OWED or the total price: that's eight pound forty, that'll be five euros, it comes to twelve pounds, that's ten dollars altogether.
positives: That's eight pound forty altogether.
That'll be five euros, please.
It comes to twelve pounds fifty.
That's three pounds for the coffee.
Altogether that's twenty dollars.

near_misses.text: I paid ten pounds for it.
It's about three or four miles.
near_misses.why: an amount, but not money owed
complaint about price, no total stated

boundary: Must state a sum of money the hearer owes or the total of a transaction.

frames.name: read-back receipt
frames.shape: [REPEATED INSTRUCTION] . got it | understood | will do
frames.definition: The speaker MARKS RECEIPT of an instruction or information, often by saying it back: got it, understood, noted, that's right, exactly right, word perfect (confirming the other's read-back), OK so I take two after food.
positives: Got it. Two tablets after breakfast.
Understood.
That's right, two after each meal.
Word perfect.
Noted, I'll bring it on Monday.

near_misses.why: asks for receipt, does not mark it

near_misses.text: That's right next to the bank.

boundary: Confirming the OTHER's correct read-back ('that's right', 'exactly right', 'word perfect') counts.
A bare 'OK' or 'right' as a discourse marker does not fire.

frames.name: reassurance / normalising
frames.shape: don't worry | that's normal | you're doing [ADV]
frames.definition: The speaker REASSURES the other or normalises their worry or trouble: don't worry, nothing to worry about, that's (completely) normal, you're doing fine/well/marvellous, it's fine/alright/okay (said to reassure), not at all / no trouble / no problem (as a downgrade of thanks or apology).
positives: Don't worry - there's a lot of us to remember.
That's completely normal after an operation.
A year? Well, you're doing marvellous.
Not at all, it was a pleasure.
That's alright - just breathe normally.

near_misses.text: Is it alright if I sit here?

boundary: Must be addressed to the other to ease worry, embarrassment or thanks.

frames.name: compliance commitment
frames.definition: The speaker COMMITS to do what was asked, advised or agreed: I will, will do, righto, right you are, deal, I'll do that, I promise, I'll bring it on Monday (agreeing to a request).
positives: Righto. Thank you, love.
Will do.
I will, thank you.
Deal. See you on Saturday.
I promise I'll take them with food.

near_misses.why: prediction about the speaker, no commitment

near_misses.text: We'll do it again after tea.
near_misses.why: the speaker announces a plan to the other, not compliance with their request

boundary: The commitment responds to a request, instruction, advice or proposal from the other (stated or clearly implied by the turn).
Orders with 'I'll have' do not fire.
